source.title_on_document: Examining Human-AI Collaboration for Co-Writing Constructive Comments Online

supplement.where: Appendix A, PDF pp. 30-33; no separate external supplement identified.
supplement.holds: Thread titles, generation settings and prompts, and Tables 11-20. Tables 15 and 17 contain pairwise and signed-rank statistics; Tables 16 and 18 contain length-adjusted ANCOVA tests; Table 19 gives country-specific output means. Between-writer similarity results are in main-text Table 8 (p. 18). No participant-level SDs, SEs, or confidence intervals for diversity contrasts are supplied.

paper_design_summary: After a stimulus-validation study and a small pilot, Indian and US participants judged supplied LLM-generated comments in a perception experiment, without receiving AI writing assistance. A separate Prolific writing experiment randomly assigned people to independent writing or revising their drafts with GPT-4, with 103 writers in the completed sample (pp. 2, 10-12). Final comments were scored by independent judges and computational measures of constructiveness and similarity across writers; fixed-order initial-to-final comparisons within the AI arm were also reported (pp. 12, 14-19).

studies.label: Phase 1 preparatory validation of argumentation styles

assignment.what_was_assigned: Random selection of threads and LLM-generated comments for annotation; neutral annotators also received randomly selected stances. No assignment of AI writing assistance.
assignment.quote: we showed them either one randomly selected homophobic or Islamophobic thread, along with four randomly selected LLM-generated comments written for that thread.

participants.exclusions: No participant exclusions stated. Incorrectly labeled or disputed comments were regenerated; these are stimulus changes, not exclusions of people (p. 8).
participants.who: MTurk annotators, not writers receiving assistance. Table 2 reports US: 142 and India: 88 annotators.
participants.quote: we conducted a validation study with 230 crowd workers from MTurk in India and the US.

ai_tool.how_used: Researchers generated logical and dialectical comments for human annotation; annotators did not co-write comments (pp. 7-9, Section 3.1).

task.description: Classify the argumentation style of supplied LLM-generated comments. Four comments per annotator (pp. 7-9, Section 3.1).

studies.label: Phase 1 preparatory pilot of constructiveness explanations

assignment.what_was_assigned: A preceding pilot collected open-ended explanations; assignment procedure is not described.
assignment.locator: p. 10, Section 3.1, paragraph preceding the list of characteristics

participants.exclusions: Not stated; only country counts for participants providing pilot explanations are given.
participants.who: Pilot participants: US: 27; India: 22. Total is the sum of these explicitly reported counts. Recruitment platform not stated for the pilot.
participants.quote: a small pilot (US: 27, India: 22) preceding the main experiment

ai_tool.how_used: No AI-assisted production task is described for this pilot; its specific model use is not stated.

task.description: Provide open-ended explanations for perceived constructiveness, used to inform response options in the main perception experiment (p. 10, Section 3.1).

assignment.what_was_assigned: Threads, comment sampling, and position within pairs randomized. Both alternatives were LLM-generated stimuli; people judged supplied comments, without receiving writing assistance.
assignment.quote: Participants saw each comment only in one pair, and the order of comments within each pair was randomized.

arms.name: Logical LLM-generated comments
arms.description: One logical comment in each pair; the same judges also saw dialectical comments.

arms.name: Dialectical LLM-generated comments
arms.description: One dialectical comment in each pair; stance and thread matched within the pair.

participants.exclusions: Four attention-check failures excluded. Initial country counts: US: 51, India: 52 (p. 9); retained: US: 50, India: 49 (p. 10). Recruitment/participation counts are not treated as explicitly reported assignment counts.
participants.who: Prolific judges. Retained sample: US: 50; India: 49 (Table 4). Total 99 is the sum, also consistent with 103 participants minus four exclusions.
participants.quote: In total, 103 people participated in the study. We removed responses from four participants, who failed the attention check.

ai_tool.how_used: GPT-4 generated stimuli and separately performed the judgment task. Human participants evaluated supplied outputs without AI writing assistance (pp. 7-10, Section 3.1).

task.description: Choose the more constructive comment and explain why for four logical-versus-dialectical pairs on a homophobic or Islamophobic thread (pp. 9-10).

assignment.what_was_assigned: Individual writers assigned between subjects to writing without external assistance or GPT-4 revision assistance. Thread order and prompt order also randomized.
assignment.quote: We designed a between-subjects experiment where participants were randomly assigned to either a control or a test group.
assignment.locator: p. 10, Section 3.2, Writing Task; p. 11, prompt-order description

arms.name: Human-written comments (control)
arms.description: Independent writing without Internet or ChatGPT; 104 comments collected. People counts per arm not explicitly reported (pp. 10, 12).

arms.name: HAI-written comments (test)
arms.description: Draft first, request at least one GPT-4 rewrite, then accept, reject, regenerate, or edit. There were 102 final comments, not 102 people (pp. 10-12 and Figure 2).

participants.exclusions: Recruitment lists 52 Indian and 52 US writers; Table 5 lists 51 Indian and 52 US completers. The missing Indian participant and timing of loss relative to assignment are unexplained. Assignment and per-arm people counts remain null. The p. 16 claim that 87 participants incorporated suggestions is inconsistent with the writing sample/output counts and is not used as a people count.
participants.who: Prolific writers not in Phase 1. Table 5 lists 52 US and 51 Indian completers; p. 2 explicitly describes 103 Phase 2 participants. Separate scoring judges are not added to this writer sample.
participants.quote: a different set of 103 Indian and American crowd workers on Prolific.
participants.locator: p. 2, Introduction; p. 12, Section 3.2, Participant Recruitment, and Table 5

ai_tool.how_used: Draft at least 20 words, then select provided prompts or write a custom prompt; at least one model request required. The rewriting prompt included thread, country, stance, and draft. Participants could accept, reject, regenerate, or edit (pp. 10-11 and Figure 2). Appendix generation settings refer to Phase 1 stimuli; applicability to the live revision interface is not stated.

task.description: Write a constructive comment of at least 50 words on each of one homophobic and one Islamophobic thread relevant to the country. In scope because outputs are compared across writers for similarity (p. 10; pp. 17-19, Section 4.2.3).
task.duration: No fixed time limit stated. Observed average writing time: test 5.17 minutes; control 6.71 minutes (p. 16, Section 4.2.1).

outcomes.name: Human-rated constructiveness of final comments
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Independent Prolific judges selected the more constructive comment in stance- and thread-matched pairs. There were 401 HAI-versus-Human pair judgments (p. 14). Across all comment-source comparisons, 157 judges supplied 727 evaluations after seven attention-check exclusions (p. 12). They are raters, not writers. The printed chi-square N=802 is not a people count. No adjustment for repeated writers, comments, or raters is stated. The fully AI-generated comparisons are not the randomized assistance contrast.

contrasts.reported: HAI was chosen as more constructive in 64% of cases versus Human in 36%; chi-square(1, N=802)=62.56, p<0.000005, phi=0.28, odds ratio=3.19. Chi-square tests used Bonferroni corrections.
contrasts.locator: pp. 14-15, Section 4.2.1; p. 15, Table 6 and Figure 4

outcomes.name: Between-writer semantic similarity
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Between-writer comparison in Section 4.2.3, distinct from initial-to-final similarity in Section 4.2.2. The paper identifies all-MiniLM-L6-v2 for semantic similarity in Section 3.2 (p. 12); Section 4.2.3 does not restate a model. Arm averages, but no SD, SE, CI, or exact p-value, are printed.

contrasts.reported: Human-written comments (control): 0.41; HAI-written comments (test): 0.42. The table prints a dash for the test statistics; the text reports no significant difference.
contrasts.locator: pp. 17-19, Section 4.2.3; p. 18, Table 8

diversity_detail.computed_over: Comments by different participants within the same arm, on the same thread and sharing the same stance; exact pair enumeration and analyzed pair counts are not reported (p. 17, Section 4.2.3).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Multiple Mann-Whitney U tests with Bonferroni corrections (p. 18, Table 8 and text); no participant-clustered precision or adjustment for dependence among pairs sharing comments is reported.
diversity_detail.notes: Similarity is inverse to diversity. No standardized mean difference, SD, SE, or CI is supplied. Pair counts and handling of shared participants are unclear; printed tests do not establish independent-participant precision.

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: No reuse of participants from another paper reported. Within this paper, writers are explicitly separate from Phase 1, and Phase 2 scoring judges are separate from writers and Phase 1 participants. Pure-AI comparisons reuse Phase 1 model-generated comments, not another human sample.

sample_overlap.locator: p. 12, Section 3.2, Participant Recruitment and Human Evaluation of Constructiveness; p. 14, Section 4.2

company_involvement.description: The authors acknowledge support from Infosys and the Cornell Global AI initiative. Nature or amount of company support and any role in design or analysis are not stated.

eligibility.reason: Phase 2 (S4) randomly assigns individual people to GPT-4 assistance versus no external assistance (p. 10, Section 3.2), with 103 analyzed/completing writers stated in the Introduction and represented in Table 5 (p. 2; p. 12). It computes similarity among final comments by different participants within conditions, matched on thread and stance (pp. 17-19, Section 4.2.3 and Table 8). Writing compared across writers for similarity is in scope. AI remains available during final production (p. 11, Figure 2). Auxiliary annotators, pilot participants, perception judges, and scoring judges are not added to the eligibility denominator. Distinct-2/TTR aggregation is unclear, but explicitly between-writer cosine, semantic, and ROUGE-L analyses independently meet the scored-output criterion.

one_line_finding: Among 103 writers, AI assistance produced no significant change in between-writer semantic similarity (HAI 0.42 vs. control 0.41) but lower ROUGE-L overlap (0.16 vs. 0.18; p<0.001), with HAI comments preferred as more constructive in 64% of paired judgments (p. 2; p. 12, Table 5; p. 18, Table 8; p. 15, Figure 4).
open_questions: What happened to the additional recruited Indian writer? Recruitment lists 52 Indian and 52 US writers; Table 5 lists 51 Indian and 52 US completers. Assignment and per-arm people counts are not reported (p. 12).
Does the revision subset count of 87 denote comments or people? Page 16 calls them participants, inconsistent with the writing sample and test-group output count; no subset denominator is inferred.

Were Distinct-2 and TTR computed within individual comments or on pooled comments, and what were the independent units for their Mann-Whitney tests? The text does not establish between-person diversity (pp. 18-19, Table 8).

How many between-writer pairs entered each similarity test, and how were dependencies from shared comments/writers handled? No participant-level SE, bootstrap, or clustered analysis is reported (pp. 17-19).

The scoring survey says each participant reviewed four pairs, yet reports 727 evaluations from 157 retained judges (p. 12). The chi-square N=802 for HAI versus Human differs from the 401 pair judgments on p. 14; these are not people counts, and test construction needs clarification (p. 15, Table 6).
Is a study dataset or analysis script available? Third-party tool links are given, but no study-specific data or code URL.
notes: Screened on 2026-10-09 using the entire markdown, including references and Appendix, followed by PyMuPDF text and table checks. Locators use physical PDF pages, matching article pages 410:1-410:33. Four study entries distinguish the explicitly described preparatory validation study, preparatory pilot, main Phase 1 perception experiment, and Phase 2 writing experiment; only S4 establishes core eligibility. The independent Phase 2 human-evaluation survey is treated as the scoring procedure for S4 outputs rather than a new writing intervention or independent creative-producer sample. The largest recorded human cohort is therefore 230 annotators in S1; the eligible randomized writer sample is 103. S2 total 49 and S3 total 99 are exact sums of printed country counts, not inferred from comments; S3 also agrees with the participant total minus stated exclusions. No per-arm writer counts are derived by dividing output counts. The abstract total of 600 is not used as a single-study sample. Table 2 reports 39 US validated comments, whereas the finalized US stimulus pool is stated to contain 32 (pp. 8-9); this does not alter the reported annotator count. The main 15 relevant output outcomes are listed, prioritizing human-rated quality and homogeneity measures. Omitted from separate outcomes: named-entity counts (p. 9, Table 3; p. 18, Figure 6F; pp. 32-33, Tables 15, 17, 19); initial-to-final retention assessed with semantic similarity, BERTScore, and cosine similarity (pp. 16-18, Section 4.2.2 and Figure 6A); and descriptive manual coding of opinion distortion (p. 19, Section 4.2.4). Within-person retention is not across_people diversity. Self-reported ownership, satisfaction, difficulty, prompt choices, and writing time are not scored-on-output creativity outcomes. Pure-AI-versus-human and pure-AI-versus-HAI comparisons use researcher-generated outputs and are not randomized assistance contrasts. Phase 1 perception/validation outcomes answer none of the three atlas questions, so their outcome arrays are empty. All draft-to-final and editing contrasts occur within the assisted session, without AI removal, and do not measure after_ai. No preregistration or explicit primary-outcome designation was found. Reported test statistics, p thresholds, r, phi, odds ratio, and ANCOVA eta-squared are copied rather than converted. The statistics_available value none can accompany printed averages where the vocabulary has no means-only category; it does not imply no descriptive values. Null units for Distinct-2 and TTR preserve unreported aggregation. No standardized mean differences or standard errors were computed.
